claim: Microorganisms produce numerous secondary metabolites (SMs) with various biological activities.
source: Microorganisms produce numerous secondary metabolites (SMs) with various biological activities.
evidence: This is a general statement about microbial secondary metabolites that is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Many secondary metabolite encoding gene clusters are silent under standard laboratory conditions because for their activation they need the ecological context, such as the presence of other microorganisms.
source: Many of their encoding gene clusters are silent under standard laboratory conditions because for their activation they need the ecological context, such as the presence of other microorganisms.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in microbial secondary metabolism and is also supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: A silent gene cluster of Aspergillus fumigatus is activated by the bacterium Streptomyces rapamycinicus during bacterial-fungal interaction.
source: Here, we report the identification of an as-yet uncharacterized silent gene cluster of the fungus Aspergillus fumigatus, which is activated by the bacterium Streptomyces rapamycinicus during the bacterial-fungal interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating upregulation of cluster genes during co-cultivation.

claim: The novel fungal metabolite fumigermin is produced when A. fumigatus is activated by S. rapamycinicus.
source: The resulting natural product is the novel fungal metabolite fumigermin, the biosynthesis of which requires the polyketide synthase FgnA.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data in Figure 1A showing the presence of compound 1 (fumigermin) in co-culture.

claim: Fumigermin biosynthesis requires the polyketide synthase FgnA.
source: The resulting natural product is the novel fungal metabolite fumigermin, the biosynthesis of which requires the polyketide synthase FgnA.
evidence: This is supported by deletion mutant data in Figure 1D showing loss of fumigermin production in ΔfgnA strain.

claim: Fumigermin inhibits germination of spores of the inducing S. rapamycinicus.
source: Fumigermin inhibits germination of spores of the inducing S. rapamycinicus, and thus helps the fungus to defend resources in the shared habitat against a bacterial competitor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A and 3B showing dose-dependent inhibition of S. rapamycinicus spore germination.

claim: Fumigermin helps the fungus to defend resources in the shared habitat against a bacterial competitor.
source: Fumigermin inhibits germination of spores of the inducing S. rapamycinicus, and thus helps the fungus to defend resources in the shared habitat against a bacterial competitor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed germination inhibition activity and the ecological context of the interaction.

claim: Microorganisms interact with neighboring species in mutualistic or antagonistic ways in their ecological niche.
source: In their ecological niche, microorganisms interact with neighboring species in mutualistic or antagonistic ways.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and is cited in the introduction.

claim: Microorganisms rely on chemical compounds for many of their communication processes.
source: For many of their communication processes, they rely on chemical compounds (Mithöfer and Boland, 2016), often belonging to the group of secondary metabolites (SMs) (Keller et al., 2005; Clardy et al., 2009; Brakhage, 2013; Netzker et al., 2015; Keller, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Chemical compounds used for microbial communication often belong to the group of secondary metabolites.
source: For many of their communication processes, they rely on chemical compounds (Mithöfer and Boland, 2016), often belonging to the group of secondary metabolites (SMs) (Keller et al., 2005; Clardy et al., 2009; Brakhage, 2013; Netzker et al., 2015; Keller, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Secondary metabolites show high chemical diversity.
source: SMs show high chemical diversity, and their encoding genes mostly cluster together in a particular genomic locus (Smith et al., 1990; Trail et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations.

claim: Secondary metabolite encoding genes mostly cluster together in a particular genomic locus.
source: SMs show high chemical diversity, and their encoding genes mostly cluster together in a particular genomic locus (Smith et al., 1990; Trail et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The biosynthesis of secondary metabolites is regulated at various levels to ensure production of SMs in a relevant context.
source: The biosynthesis of SMs is regulated at various levels to ensure production of SMs in a relevant context (Brakhage, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Interactions of neighboring microorganisms have been identified as triggers of secondary metabolite production.
source: Several environmental signals have been identified as triggers of SM production, such as interactions of neighboring microorganisms (Künzler, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Biosynthetic gene clusters are often not expressed in laboratory settings where natural triggers of SM production are missing.
source: In the artificial setting of a laboratory where natural triggers of SM production are missing, biosynthetic gene clusters are often not expressed and therefore their corresponding SMs remain undetectable (Bergmann et al., 2007; Brakhage, 2013; Rutledge and Challis, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Microbial co-culturing has proven to be particularly successful in stimulating microbial SM discovery.
source: One approach that has proven to be particularly successful in stimulating microbial SM discovery, as well as avoiding redundancy often leading to re-isolation of known compounds, is mimicking the settings of a particular ecological niche through microbial co-culturing (Netzker et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Competitive inter-kingdom interactions have been exploited as a trigger for production of bioactive compounds.
source: In particular, competitive inter-kingdom interactions have been exploited as a trigger for production of bioactive compounds (Watanabe et al., 1982; Cueto et al., 2001; Moree et al., 2013; Khalil et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Several studies have reported the induction of compound biosynthesis in Aspergillus spp. by Streptomyces.
source: For example, several studies have reported the induction of compound biosynthesis in Aspergillus spp. by Streptomyces (Schroeckh et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2016) or by Mycobacterium sp. (Jomori et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Downregulation of fungal metabolite biosynthesis by Streptomyces spp. was reported.
source: Conversely, downregulation of fungal metabolite biosynthesis by Streptomyces spp. was also reported (Verheecke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: An inter-kingdom interaction between the soil-dwelling actinomycete Streptomyces rapamycinicus and the filamentous fungus Aspergillus nidulans was discovered in previous work.
source: In our previous work, we discovered an inter-kingdom interaction between the soil-dwelling actinomycete Streptomyces rapamycinicus and the filamentous fungus Aspergillus nidulans (Schroeckh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: The silent SM gene cluster encoding biosynthesis of orsellinic acid and its derivatives in A. nidulans is activated on physical contact of the fungus with S. rapamycinicus.
source: We showed that the silent SM gene cluster encoding biosynthesis of orsellinic acid and its derivatives in A. nidulans is activated on physical contact of the fungus with the bacterium (Schroeckh et al., 2009; Nützmann et al., 2011; Fischer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research by the authors.

claim: S. rapamycinicus triggers expression of the silent polyketide gene cluster encoding the C-prenylated fumicyclines in A. fumigatus.
source: We subsequently showed that the same bacterial strain also engaged in intimate interplay with the fungus A. fumigatus, in this case triggering expression of the silent polyketide gene cluster encoding the C-prenylated fumicyclines (König et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: A new metabolite (1) was detected in the mixed fermentation of A. fumigatus ATCC 46645 and S. rapamycinicus, but not after the addition of supernatant of an S. rapamycinicus culture to the fungal culture.
source: Using LC-MS analysis, we detected a new metabolite (1) in the mixed fermentation of A. fumigatus ATCC 46645 and S. rapamycinicus, but not after the addition of supernatant of an S. rapamycinicus culture to the fungal culture (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Other streptomycetes such as S. iranensis, S. coelicolor or S. lividans also induced the production of compound 1 during co-cultivation, but to a much lesser extent.
source: Other streptomycetes such as S. iranensis, S. coelicolor or S. lividans also induced the production of compound 1 during co-cultivation, but to a much lesser extent (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Compound 1 has a molecular weight of m/z 194 amu.
source: For compound 1 a molecular weight of m/z 194 amu was detected.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: Compound 1 has a molecular formula of C11H14O3.
source: A molecular formula of C11H14O3 was determined by HRESI-MS.
evidence: This is supported by high-resolution mass spectrometry data.

claim: Compound 1 represents an α-pyrone and was named fumigermin.
source: Compound 1 represents an α-pyrone and was named fumigermin (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by NMR structural elucidation data shown in Figure 1B and supplementary figures.

claim: Fumigermin is structurally similar to nectriapyrone from Piricularia oryzae.
source: It is structurally similar to other microbial α-pyrones, including the fungal SMs nectriapyrone from Piricularia oryzae (Motoyama et al., 2019) and gibepyrone produced by Fusarium fujikuroi (Janevska et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and citations to previous research.

claim: Fumigermin is structurally similar to gibepyrone produced by Fusarium fujikuroi.
source: It is structurally similar to other microbial α-pyrones, including the fungal SMs nectriapyrone from Piricularia oryzae (Motoyama et al., 2019) and gibepyrone produced by Fusarium fujikuroi (Janevska et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and citations to previous research.

claim: Fumigermin is structurally similar to the bacterial germicidins originally isolated from Streptomyces viridochromogens.
source: It is also similar to the bacterial germicidins (Figure 2C) originally isolated from Streptomyces viridochromogens (Aoki et al., 2011), but also produced by Streptomyces species S. coelicolor and S. lividans (Song et al., 2006; Chemler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2C and citations to previous research.

claim: The steady-state mRNA levels of the putative cluster genes of A. fumigatus ATCC 46645, including gene Afu1g01010, were markedly upregulated during co-cultivation of A. fumigatus ATCC 46645 with S. rapamycinicus.
source: As indicated in Figure 1C, the steady-state mRNA levels of the putative cluster genes of A. fumigatus ATCC 46645, including gene Afu1g01010, were markedly upregulated during co-cultivation of A. fumigatus ATCC 46645 with S. rapamycinicus.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Production of fumigermin (1) was fully abolished in the deletion mutant of Afu1g01010 during co-cultivation with S. rapamycinicus.
source: LC-MS monitoring of the co-cultivation of the resulting deletion mutant with S. rapamycinicus demonstrated that production of fumigermin (1) was fully abolished (Figure 1D), confirming that the PKS gene Afu1g01010 is involved in its biosynthesis.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Overexpressing Afu1g01010 using the inducible tetOn promoter system in A. fumigatus ATCC 46645 led to the appearance of fumigermin under inducing conditions in the absence of bacteria.
source: This was further proven by overexpressing Afu1g01010, hereby named fgnA, using the inducible tetOn promoter system in A. fumigatus ATCC 46645, which led to the appearance of fumigermin under inducing conditions in the absence of bacteria (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Metabolic profiling of the culture of A. nidulans overexpressing the fgnA gene of strain ATCC 46645 revealed the formation of 1, a metabolite identical to fumigermin.
source: Metabolic profiling of the culture of A. nidulans overexpressing the fgnA gene of strain ATCC 46645 revealed the formation of 1, a metabolite identical to fumigermin which had been previously detected during the co-cultivation of A. fumigatus and S. rapamycinicus (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Fumigermin is a direct product of the encoded polyketide synthase FgnA of A. fumigatus.
source: This finding suggested that fumigermin, that is compound 1, is a direct product of the encoded polyketide synthase FgnA of A. fumigatus.
evidence: This is inferred from the heterologous expression data showing that fgnA alone is sufficient to produce fumigermin.

claim: Although all cluster proteins were produced in the heterologous strain, no further compound, other than fumigermin, was detected in the heterologous expression strain.
source: Although all cluster proteins were produced in the heterologous strain, as evidenced by the fluorescent signal localized to the nuclei (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and additionally supported by label-free proteomic analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), no further compound, other than fumigermin, was detected in the heterologous expression strain (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy, proteomic analysis, and LC-MS data shown in Figure 2A and supplementary figures.

claim: The additional enzymes do not modify the chemical product of FgnA, even when co-expressed with the functional FgnA PKS.
source: This result indicates that the additional enzymes do not modify the chemical product of FgnA, even when co-expressed with the functional FgnA PKS.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that expressing the entire cluster did not produce any compounds other than fumigermin.

claim: The deduced amino acid sequence of FgnA contains a ketosynthase (KS), acyltransferase (AT), dehydratase (DH), methyl transferase (MT), ketoreductase (KR) and an acyl-carrier protein (ACP) domain.
source: The deduced amino acid sequence of FgnA analyzed by CD-search (Marchler-Bauer and Bryant, 2004) revealed the presence of a ketosynthase (KS), acyltransferase (AT), dehydratase (DH), methyl transferase (MT), ketoreductase (KR) and an acyl-carrier protein (ACP) domain, classifying this enzyme as a partially reducing PKS (Cox, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis using CD-search and citation to previous research.

claim: FgnA is classified as a partially reducing PKS.
source: The deduced amino acid sequence of FgnA analyzed by CD-search (Marchler-Bauer and Bryant, 2004) revealed the presence of a ketosynthase (KS), acyltransferase (AT), dehydratase (DH), methyl transferase (MT), ketoreductase (KR) and an acyl-carrier protein (ACP) domain, classifying this enzyme as a partially reducing PKS (Cox, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by domain analysis and citation to previous research.

claim: Eight carbon atoms of fumigermin originate from acetate.
source: Isotope labeling studies using (2-13C)acetate and (methyl-13C)methionine showed that eight carbon atoms of fumigermin originate from acetate, while the remaining three carbons derived from S-adenosyl methionine, agreeing with the existence of an MT domain in the PKS (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by isotope labeling experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The remaining three carbons of fumigermin derived from S-adenosyl methionine.
source: Isotope labeling studies using (2-13C)acetate and (methyl-13C)methionine showed that eight carbon atoms of fumigermin originate from acetate, while the remaining three carbons derived from S-adenosyl methionine, agreeing with the existence of an MT domain in the PKS (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by isotope labeling experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Among Aspergillus spp., the fgn cluster is unique to A. fumigatus and the closely related species A. novofumigatus.
source: Among Aspergillus spp., the fgn cluster is unique to A. fumigatus and the closely related species A. novofumigatus (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The cluster is rarely found in the different sequenced A. fumigatus genomes.
source: Moreover, the cluster is rarely found in the different sequenced A. fumigatus genomes, which is consistent with a previously reported analysis of clusters in various A. fumigatus isolates (Lind et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis and citation to previous research.

claim: Amongst the A. fumigatus strains harboring the fgn cluster, production of fumigermin was restricted to strain ATCC 46645.
source: Amongst the A. fumigatus strains harboring the fgn cluster, production of fumigermin was restricted to strain ATCC 46645.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Fumigermin could not be detected in a co-culture of S. rapamycinicus with other A. fumigatus strains, such as Af293 and A1163, or A. novofumigatus IBT 16806.
source: We could not detect fumigermin in a co-culture of S. rapamycinicus with other A. fumigatus strains, such as Af293 and A1163, or A. novofumigatus IBT 16806 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The fgnA gene of strains Af293 and IBT 16806 contained several missense SNPs.
source: As indicated by the gene sequences, the corresponding fgnA gene of strains Af293 and IBT 16806 contained several missense SNPs, while that of strain A1163 had undergone a chromosomal breakage around 800 bp from the start codon of fgnA, and contained a C → T missense mutation at position 272 (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by DNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The fgnA gene of strain A1163 had undergone a chromosomal breakage around 800 bp from the start codon of fgnA.
source: As indicated by the gene sequences, the corresponding fgnA gene of strains Af293 and IBT 16806 contained several missense SNPs, while that of strain A1163 had undergone a chromosomal breakage around 800 bp from the start codon of fgnA, and contained a C → T missense mutation at position 272 (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by DNA sequencing and PCR data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The fgnA gene of strain A1163 contained a C → T missense mutation at position 272.
source: As indicated by the gene sequences, the corresponding fgnA gene of strains Af293 and IBT 16806 contained several missense SNPs, while that of strain A1163 had undergone a chromosomal breakage around 800 bp from the start codon of fgnA, and contained a C → T missense mutation at position 272 (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by DNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Neither FgnA PKS from Af293 nor A1163 was able to produce fumigermin when overexpressed in A. nidulans.
source: To further verify the assumption that the fgnA genes are not functional in several A. fumigatus strains, we overexpressed the fgnA genes of both the Af293 and A1163 strains in A. nidulans. As predicted, neither FgnA PKS was able to produce fumigermin (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The heterologous overexpression of the 'repaired' fgnA gene in A. nidulans under the control of the gpdA promoter led to formation of the expected polyketide metabolite fumigermin.
source: The heterologous overexpression of the resulting 'repaired' fgnA gene in A. nidulans under the control of the gpdA promoter led to formation of the expected polyketide metabolite fumigermin, confirming that this reconstruction functionally rescued the 'inactive' A1163 fgnA gene and led to production of the previously observed metabolite derived from the fgnA gene (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Additional orthologs of the entire fgn cluster are found in distantly related fungi such as Parastagonopora nodorum, Pseudogymnoascus pannorum, Escovopsis weberi, and Hypoxylon sp.
source: The obtained data indicate that additional orthologs of the entire fgn cluster are found in distantly related fungi such as the major pathogen of wheat Parastagonopora nodorum from the fungal taxon Dothideomycetes (Hane et al., 2007), the bat pathogen Pseudogymnoascus pannorum which belongs to the Leotiomycetes (Minnis and Lindner, 2013) and fungi of the Sodariomycetes such as the parasitic microfungus Escovopsis weberi (Reynolds and Currie, 2004) and the endophyte Hypoxylon sp. (Hsieh et al., 2005; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and database searches, with citations to previous research.

claim: It is conceivable that the fgn cluster was spread between different fungal species through horizontal gene transfer.
source: As these microorganisms are derived from different fungal classes and occupy diverse habitats, it is conceivable that the fgn cluster was spread between different fungal species through horizontal gene transfer.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the phylogenetic distribution of the cluster.

claim: A similarity search based on the protein sequence of FgnA did not retrieve the stand-alone PKS enzymes Nec1 and Gpy1.
source: Surprisingly, a similarity search based on the protein sequence of FgnA did not retrieve the stand-alone PKS enzymes Nec1 and Gpy1, which catalyze the biosynthesis of the structurally similar microbial SMs nectriapyrone (Figure 2—figure supplement 4; Janevska et al., 2016) and gibepyrone (Motoyama et al., 2019), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis and citations to previous research.

claim: Nec1 and Gpy1 are not orthologs of FgnA, and show low similarity to FgnA at the amino acid level.
source: Despite also being classified as fungal iterative type I PKS, Nec1 and Gpy1 are not orthologs of FgnA, and show low similarity to FgnA at the amino acid level.
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison analysis.

claim: The number of germinated S. rapamycinicus spores was drastically reduced by fumigermin in a dose-dependent manner.
source: As shown in Figure 3A and B, the number of germinated S. rapamycinicus spores was drastically reduced by fumigermin in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Fumigermin and germicidin B showed the same anti-germination effect against spores of S. rapamycinicus.
source: A comparison of fumigermin and germicidin B demonstrated that both compounds showed the same anti-germination effect against spores of S. rapamycinicus (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Fumigermin inhibited germination of S. rapamyinicus spores out of solid medium.
source: Moreover, fumigermin also inhibited germination of S. rapamyinicus spores out of solid medium (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The spores' ability to germinate and form a mycelial network was regained after washing and re-cultivation in fresh media.
source: To reveal whether the inhibition of spore germination was reversible, we incubated S. rapamycinicus spores with fumigermin for 90 h, and subsequently washed and re-cultivated the spores in fresh media. As shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, the spores' ability to germinate and form a mycelial network was regained.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fumigermin is a reversible germination inhibitor.
source: Thus, fumigermin is a reversible germination inhibitor, which keeps S. rapamycinicus spores in a dormant state and leaves them ungerminated as long as the compound is present.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that spores regain germination ability after washing away fumigermin.

claim: Fumigermin keeps S. rapamycinicus spores in a dormant state and leaves them ungerminated as long as the compound is present.
source: Thus, fumigermin is a reversible germination inhibitor, which keeps S. rapamycinicus spores in a dormant state and leaves them ungerminated as long as the compound is present.
evidence: This is inferred from the germination inhibition and reversibility experiments.

claim: Fumigermin could be re-purified from 90 h-old supernatant of a fumigermin-treated S. rapamycinicus spore sample, and further re-used to inhibit germination of fresh S. rapamycinicus spores.
source: Notably, fumigermin could be re-purified from 90 h-old supernatant of a fumigermin-treated S. rapamycinicus spore sample, and further re-used to inhibit germination of fresh S. rapamycinicus spores (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The finding that fumigermin can be re-purified and re-used points towards high stability of the compound.
source: This finding points towards high stability of the compound.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that fumigermin can be recovered and reused.

claim: The germination of S. coelicolor and S. lividans was only slightly inhibited when treated with fumigermin.
source: The germination of S. coelicolor and S. lividans was only slightly inhibited when treated with fumigermin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Moderate germination inhibition was observed for S. coelicolor treated with the rather high concentration of 1000 µg/mL fumigermin.
source: Moderate germination inhibition was observed for S. coelicolor treated with the rather high concentration of 1000 µg/mL fumigermin (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The inhibitory effect of fumigermin was lost after 3 days of incubation with S. coelicolor.
source: The inhibitory effect was lost after 3 days of incubation with the compound, suggesting that fumigermin might be degraded by this Streptomyces spp.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation and leads to speculation about degradation.

claim: None of the streptomycetes tested was able to degrade fumigermin.
source: The analysis showed that none of the streptomycetes tested was able to degrade fumigermin, which was in contrast to the P. aeruginosa PAO1 control culture where fumigermin was almost depleted in the culture supernatant.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: P. aeruginosa PAO1 was able to degrade fumigermin.
source: The analysis showed that none of the streptomycetes tested was able to degrade fumigermin, which was in contrast to the P. aeruginosa PAO1 control culture where fumigermin was almost depleted in the culture supernatant.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Fumigermin had no obvious effect on the fitness of the producing isolate A. fumigatus ATCC 46645 at least when cultivated in monoculture.
source: As expected, fumigermin had no obvious effect on the fitness of the producing isolate A. fumigatus ATCC 46645 at least when cultivated in monoculture (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observation, though data are not shown.

claim: Fumigermin is not produced in an axenic A. fumigatus ATCC 46645 culture.
source: Consistently, fumigermin is not produced in an axenic A. fumigatus ATCC 46645 culture, but is produced in high amounts and excreted by A. fumigatus ATCC 46645 when co-cultured with S. rapamycinicus.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Fumigermin is produced in high amounts and excreted by A. fumigatus ATCC 46645 when co-cultured with S. rapamycinicus.
source: Consistently, fumigermin is not produced in an axenic A. fumigatus ATCC 46645 culture, but is produced in high amounts and excreted by A. fumigatus ATCC 46645 when co-cultured with S. rapamycinicus.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Aspergillus spp., in particular A. fumigatus, and Streptomyces spp. have been isolated previously from a soil sample and found to share the same habitat.
source: Aspergillus spp., in particular A. fumigatus, and Streptomyces spp. have been isolated previously from a soil sample and found to share the same habitat (Alani et al., 2012; Khalil et al., 2019), making it likely that this laboratory scenario is also relevant for the ecological niche of the analyzed microorganisms.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A. fumigatus ATCC 46645 and S. rapamycinicus are apparently interacting in an antagonistic manner.
source: In the case of A. fumigatus ATCC 46645 and S. rapamycinicus reported here, the two microorganisms are apparently interacting in an antagonistic manner, because the fungus is triggered by the bacterium to produce the germination inhibitor fumigermin to protect its habitat's resources (Figure 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the fungus produces a compound that inhibits bacterial spore germination.

claim: As fumigermin's inhibitory activity is reversible, it is likely that the fungus does not intend to kill the bacterium.
source: As fumigermin's inhibitory activity is reversible, it is likely that the fungus does not intend to kill the bacterium.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the reversibility of the inhibition.

claim: Several Streptomyces spp. were found to induce fumigermin biosynthesis.
source: In this work, several Streptomyces spp. were found to induce fumigermin biosynthesis.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: S. iranensis is phylogenetically closely related to the fumigermin-inducer S. rapamycinicus.
source: Whereas S. iranensis is phylogenetically closely related to the fumigermin-inducer S. rapamycinicus, S. coelicolor and S. lividans are rather distantly related to S. rapamycinicus (Nouioui et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous phylogenetic research.

claim: S. coelicolor and S. lividans are rather distantly related to S. rapamycinicus.
source: Whereas S. iranensis is phylogenetically closely related to the fumigermin-inducer S. rapamycinicus, S. coelicolor and S. lividans are rather distantly related to S. rapamycinicus (Nouioui et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous phylogenetic research.

claim: Fumigermin was highly active against the main fumigermin inducers S. rapamycinicus and its close relative S. iranensis.
source: More specifically, fumigermin was highly active against the main fumigermin inducers S. rapamycinicus and its close relative S. iranensis (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observation, though data are not shown.

claim: S. coelicolor and S. lividans triggered production of lower levels of fumigermin and were not susceptible to fumigermin.
source: On the other hand, S. coelicolor and S. lividans triggered production of lower levels of fumigermin and were not susceptible to fumigermin.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data in Figure 1A and germination assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: S. coelicolor and S. lividans are known producers of the structurally related α-pyrone metabolites germicidins.
source: S. coelicolor and S. lividans are known producers of the structurally related α-pyrone metabolites germicidins (Song et al., 2006; Chemler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It is likely that S. coelicolor and S. lividans harbor an intrinsic resistance mechanism against germination-inhibiting α-pyrone compounds.
source: It is thus likely that these streptomycetes harbor an intrinsic resistance mechanism against germination-inhibiting α-pyrone compounds.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on their production of similar compounds and resistance to fumigermin.

claim: Germicidins are autoregulatory inhibitors of germination of dormant spores in a Streptomyces population.
source: Germicidins are autoregulatory inhibitors of germination of dormant spores in a Streptomyces population.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations.

claim: Germicidins presumably block the activity of a membrane located Ca2+-dependent ATPase.
source: Streptomyces germ tubes secrete germicidins, which presumably block the activity of a membrane located Ca2+-dependent ATPase (Eaton and Ensign, 1980; Grund and Ensign, 1985; Aoki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It is conceivable that A. fumigatus has acquired the ability to biosynthesize a functionally similar compound and is exploiting this effect to its advantage during interaction with the bacteria.
source: It is conceivable that A. fumigatus has acquired the ability to biosynthesize a functionally similar compound and is exploiting this effect to its advantage during interaction with the bacteria, as means of protection of the habitat's resources from competitor microorganisms.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the functional similarity to germicidins and the ecological context.

claim: Germicidins are products of a type II fatty acid synthase coupled with a bacterial type III PKS that uses precursors derived from fatty acid biosynthesis.
source: Whereas germicidins are produced by a type II fatty acid synthase coupled with a bacterial type III PKS that uses precursors derived from fatty acid biosynthesis (Figure 5 and Chemler et al., 2012), fumigermin biosynthesis involves a fungal iterative type I PKS.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Fumigermin biosynthesis involves a fungal iterative type I PKS.
source: Whereas germicidins are produced by a type II fatty acid synthase coupled with a bacterial type III PKS that uses precursors derived from fatty acid biosynthesis (Figure 5 and Chemler et al., 2012), fumigermin biosynthesis involves a fungal iterative type I PKS.
evidence: This is supported by domain analysis and experimental data.

claim: The different biosynthetic pathways of germicidins and fumigermin make a horizontal gene transfer from bacteria to fungi unlikely.
source: This finding makes a horizontal gene transfer from bacteria to fungi unlikely and rather points to a possible case of convergent evolution of the same lead structure in the bacterial and fungal kingdom.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the biosynthetic pathways are fundamentally different.

claim: The different biosynthetic pathways of germicidins and fumigermin point to a possible case of convergent evolution of the same lead structure in the bacterial and fungal kingdom.
source: This finding makes a horizontal gene transfer from bacteria to fungi unlikely and rather points to a possible case of convergent evolution of the same lead structure in the bacterial and fungal kingdom.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the structural similarity but different biosynthetic origins.

claim: It is possible that originally all five genes in the fgn cluster were functional, but that the genes encoding tailoring enzymes became inactive from mutations.
source: It is thus possible that originally all five genes were functional, but that the genes encoding tailoring enzymes became inactive from mutations, similar to the case of the fgnA gene in strains A1163 and Af293.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observation that tailoring enzymes do not modify fumigermin and the presence of mutations in fgnA in other strains.

claim: The fgn locus has been shown to be particularly prone to rearrangements and breakages, possibly as a result of being flanked by potential transposons.
source: In A. fumigatus, the fgn locus has been shown to be particularly prone to rearrangements and breakages, possibly as a result of being flanked by potential transposons (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Lind et al. have shown that the cluster 'jumped' to different genomic locations in three of the six analyzed cluster-containing strains.
source: Consistently, Lind et al. have shown that the cluster 'jumped' to different genomic locations in three of the six analyzed cluster-containing strains, in one case being located inside the fumagillin/pseurotin supercluster (Wiemann et al., 2013; Lind et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Loss of gene clusters apparently tends to occur at higher rates when they are located near telomere ends.
source: Additionally, loss of gene clusters apparently tends to occur at higher rates when they are located near telomere ends (Young et al., 2015), which might explain that the fgn cluster is only present in a few A. fumigatus isolates.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The isolate ATCC 46645 is the only Aspergillus sp. in which the cluster was maintained, even though the tailoring enzymes are apparently non-functional.
source: Our data so far indicate that the isolate ATCC 46645 is the only Aspergillus sp. in which the cluster was maintained, even though the tailoring enzymes are apparently non-functional (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only ATCC 46645 produces fumigermin and that tailoring enzymes do not modify the product.

claim: The production of fumigermin likely supported the conservation of FgnA, as it was advantageous for the particular isolate in its interaction with streptomycetes.
source: The production of fumigermin likely supported the conservation of FgnA, as it was advantageous for the particular isolate in its interaction with streptomycetes (Figure 4).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the ecological function of fumigermin.

claim: Fumigermin displayed no remarkable antimicrobial effects, except for a modest inhibitory activity against MRSA.
source: Fumigermin displayed no remarkable antimicrobial effects, except for a modest inhibitory activity against MRSA (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observation, though data are not shown.
